== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Arrays and the model program

POSITIONS.md:110
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The suites and the gate

POSITIONS.md:130
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.

#!/bin/bash
# mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads] [full]: the two microGPT checks under walk, each from an empty
# private cache (FORTRESS_CACHES) in a fresh folder under <work-dir> (old runs' folders stay; clear them by hand), each run from its own directory as its header says, both at once,
# with bin/fortress's own JVM (JAVA_FLAGS -Xmx4g -Xss64m) and FORTRESS_THREADS=<threads> (default 1).
# By default the quick pair, MicroGptFlatQuick and MicroGptAplQuick: two forward-and-backward passes each, 7 checks against the goldens,
# timeout 600 s.  With the word full in any position, the full pair, MicroGptFlatCheck and MicroGptAplCheck: 40 checks each, timeout 5400 s.
# Output to <work-dir>/<name>.txt, headed by the machine line (machine.sh) and ended by rc=.
set -u
PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatQuick.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplQuick.fss"; LIMIT=600; A=()
for a in "$@"; do
  if [ "$a" = full ]; then PROGS="explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss"; LIMIT=5400
  else A+=("$a"); fi
done
set -- "${A[@]}"
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_HOME="$(pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=${3:-1}
W=$(mkdir -p "${1:?usage}" && cd "$1" && pwd)
L=${2:?usage}
for f in $PROGS; do
  (
    t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
    R=$(mktemp -d "$W/run-$t-XXXX"); C="$R/caches"; T="$R/tmp"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"   # a fresh folder per run; nothing is deleted
    printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    {
      bash explorations/compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/machine.sh "$L $t"
      start=$(date +%s)
      ( cd "$(dirname "$f")" && FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$T" \
          timeout -k 10 $LIMIT "$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress" "$(basename "$f")" < /dev/null )
      echo "rc=$? secs=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))"
    } > "$W/$t.txt" 2>&1
  ) &
done
wait

The surveys are the evidence of that day; sections 0, 2 and 7 describe the tree as it stands, section 6 the development loop, and the order of work and the open decisions are in coordinator/PLAN.md, to which sections 4 and 5 point. Every claim cites a survey section, a file:line, a commit, or a FACTS or POSITIONS entry.

# The territory map

## 0. Terms used here

Path: one of the two execution routes, the interpreter (`fortress <file>.fss`, "walk") or the compiler (`fortress compile` then `fortress run`); "both paths" means the shared front end.

World: which prelude a run links against; the interpreter world is `FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin` + `AnyType`, the compiler world is `CompilerLibrary` + `CompilerBuiltin` + `CompilerAlgebra` + `AnyType` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:114-139`, `CompilerAlgebra` since `1bd8d3ad1`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13).

Prelude: the library a world loads without an import; the compiler world's four components are 2,405 lines against the interpreter world's 5,314 (`wc -l` of the `.fss`; `spec-to-implementation.md` §2 names the files).

Switch-over: phase 4 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, where the compiled path starts reading the interpreter's library and the compiler's own three prelude files are deleted, their tests kept (POSITIONS 2026-09-21, the library route); until then each path links its own world.

Gate: what a change must pass to land: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` at zero failures, thirteen compiled `atomic` programs three times at four threads, the ladder regression (85 files compiled and run against their baseline, the eighteen microGPT components compiled only) and the checker count, the compiled checker's errors over the interpreter's library, reported and never red on its own (protocol, hard rules; `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Counts here are from 

Shadow: a prototype of an edit to the original tree, made by compiling edited copies of the files and putting their class files ahead of the real ones on the classpath; no tracked file changes, and the gate cannot see it (`perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`; `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 3, the test classpath built from `ProjectFortress/build`).

Sealed tree: the original tree, everything outside `explorations/` and `research/`; sealed through `75cca6683` (POSITIONS 2026-09-17), editable since, each edit test first and flagged at commit (protocol, hard rules).

## 1. The five surveys, and the walkthrough beside them

`modules-and-phases.md`: the 22 packages with sizes, the import graph, the dead modules, the two pipelines phase by phase, the cache, the runtime, native interop, and the one-table divergence of the paths (B.14).

`spec-to-implementation.md`: the 53 chapters of the July 2012 draft, a table of about 110 features with the parser rule, checker class, interpreter, codegen and prelude location of each, and the layered picture of the numeric tower (§4).

`test-coverage.md`: the census of every test corpus and JUnit class, what the 1,377 and 382 are made of, the two corpora that never meet, the blind spots by module, and the loop timings.

`dormant-code.md` (part five, added at Pavol's request): the census of what is present, carries a design, and does not run: commented-out library declarations and `Library/incomplete/`, commented-out visitors and off-by-default flags in the source, commented-out test halves and the aspirational directories, the spec's genuinely dormant text and its 62 "not yet supported" notes, the papers; each item judged finished-unwired, sketch, superseded or unknown, and tied to a path step.

`design-intent-sources.md`: the five places rationale is written (in-repo papers, the Steele corpus, our extracts, the spec's draft-only notes and Internal Document, source comments and commits), a table by design area of what intent the spec leaves unstated, and its section 7, the team's word after the repository (POPL 2019, the 2012 patents, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, the sites), placed against the design areas.

`compile-path-walkthrough.md` (part six, written 2026-09-20 for the checker decisions): the compile path followed end to end, one section per stage — parsing, name resolution and grammar expansion, the checker (what it walks, what it writes, its counts on the library before climb batch 4), the desugaring switches that make the paths differ, code generation, the second JVM and the stamping class loader, native bindings in both worlds, `nat`, and a glossary.

## 2. The shape of the system, in thirteen facts

The editable surface is about 149,000 hand-written Java lines and 19,900 Scala lines; the other 535,000 Java lines are generated and checked in (counted as in `modules-and-phases.md` A.1).

The AST in `nodes/` is the only intermediate representation from parse to bytecode; there is no lower IR and no optimizing middle (B.1).

# harness fact, which the brief's role text and the fortress-repo skill carry. POSITIONS and FACTS entries are keyed
# by their numbers. Each briefing entry is its facts-extract.sh key, one line on why it is there, and CHECK where the
# record marks it (check): the checks list, read by the skeptic, a repair round and a judge, is those keys in order.
# No key holds a backslash, a backtick or a double quote, which the script refuses; facts-extract matches a heading
# without its backticks.
# Changed from lists29.py: the rungs are the record's two, A and T, in the manifest's order; the keys are each rung's
# briefing bullets in section 1, in their order, each as the record writes it, its backticks dropped and REC, PROBE
# and SNAP spelled out as section 1's opening paragraph gives them, each with the record's reason, its first letter
# capitalized; a check is marked on its entry. The forks: the record's one forks key, REC "Forks the batch takes",
# stays in each briefing as section 1 gives it, section 3's forks whole for every rung, with its (check) mark on A and
# none on T. Climb batch 29's way, each rung reading the batch's forks, its own and those of each rung beside it by the
# @WORDS filter on the heading's bold leads, does not fit this record's headings: its forks are a numbered list led
# by the fork's label (A1 to A8, T1 to T3), with no lead "For the whole batch" or "Rung A", and the section's opening

# headings do not allow 29's way cleanly). A and T share no file (section 4, "The rule the rungs keep"), and T reads

4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
7. Do the ladder regression.

## The atomic runs

The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:

    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
      done
    done

The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.

## The ladder regression

The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:

- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.
Matching ignores case, backticks and double quotes, reads curly quotes as

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It 
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.


The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' 

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the strin
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails wit
- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
  - A numeral coercion whose body spawns a task fails the component class's load: 'Thread cannot be cast to FortressTaskRunner' (ledger row 971). An operator or an argument list over two calls of the program's own functions spawns, as `small(n) - small(m)` does. Bind each call in a statement of its own, as `a = small(n)`, then `b = small(m)`, then write `a - b`.
  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral with a radix point, and `RR32` only such a numeral. So `r: RR64 = 3` is refused, and so is a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected (ledger row 442). Write `3.0`, and `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- A numeral at `=` takes its default. So `u = 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q = 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 973). `u =/= 0` and `q =/= 0.5` are then `true` (ledger row 966). Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u = z` or `u =/= z`.
- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).

content.content:
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**; its **run time** holds the tasks and the transactions. Until the **switch-over** it uses its own small library, the **prelude**; after it, the **one library**, which only walk runs today.
- A **task** is a piece of work handed to the pool of worker threads. To **fork** it is to hand it over, to **join** it is to wait for it. A **group** is the arms of a `do … also` block, the elements of a tuple or the arguments of a call, forked together. A group **completes abruptly** when an arm throws.
- A **transaction** runs an `atomic` block: its reads and writes take effect together at its **commit**, or it **aborts** and the block runs again. A **nested** block is an `atomic` block inside another.
- The **grain size** is the number of elements at which a parallel range stops splitting and runs the rest in sequence.
- The **static numerals** are his design, which climb batch 29b built (P-174, P-176). The **four numbers** are a numeral's digit count, digits after the point, radix and digits read as one integer. A **place** is where a numeral is written.
- **D1** and **D2** are the parallelism review's two questions that are his and are not yet asked: arrays of unboxed numbers inside `atomic`, and strong atomicity on the compiled path.
- A **rung** is one change, built by one worker and checked by a skeptic; a **run** is one launch of the batch workflow; the **gather** composes a run's rungs; a **guard** is a test that passes before the change and after it. The **atomic runs** are the gate's compiled programs that run three times each at four threads.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it, and its quick checks under walk stay 7 of 7 for both programs.

### The one question before the launch

**Fork G, the grain size: is it built now, with a value that cannot be measured yet?** P-175 has the one library's parallel range stop its split at a grain size, and your go of today brings the parallelism work forward. Two facts bear on it:

- Only walk runs the one library today. The value is to be measured on compiled reductions at one and four threads (P-29; PLAN's phase 6 line), and no compiled program reaches that range before the switch-over. So a value chosen now is provisional.
- A chunk run in sequence joins its elements in another order than today's tree of single elements. Under walk microGPT's reductions then round differently in their last bits. The planner tried a grain of 16: both quick checks stay 7 of 7, and the losses move by at most 4.4e-16 against a tolerance of 1e-12 (PROBES, probe 2).

The ways:

- **(a) Built now, in rung P:** the split stops at a named constant, 16 for now, and each chunk runs by the sequential range's own methods. It is tested under walk. The value is measured and set in the first batch after the switch-over. Cost: walk's microGPT numbers change in their last bits now, and once more if the measured value differs.
- **(b) Left to the first batch after the switch-over,** where PLAN had it, with its measurement. Rung P then builds the forked arguments and the joins only, and nothing changes under walk. ## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**; its **run time** holds the tasks and the transactions. Until the **switch-over** it uses its own small library, the **prelude**; after it, the **one library**, which only walk runs today.
- A **task** is a piece of work handed to the pool of worker threads. To **fork** it is to hand it over, to **join** it is to wait for it. A **group** is the arms of a `do … also` block, the elements of a tuple or the arguments of a call, forked together. A group **completes abruptly** when an arm throws.
- A **transaction** runs an `atomic` block: its reads and writes take effect together at its **commit**, or it **aborts** and the block runs again. A **nested** block is an `atomic` block inside another.
- The **grain size** is the number of elements at which a parallel range stops splitting and runs the rest in sequence.
- The **static numerals** are his design, which climb batch 29b built (P-174, P-176). The **four numbers** are a numeral's digit count, digits after the point, radix and digits read as one integer. A **place** is where a numeral is written.
- **D1** and **D2** are the parallelism review's two questions that are his and are not yet asked: arrays of unboxed numbers inside `atomic`, and strong atomicity on the compiled path.
- A **rung** is one change, built by one worker and checked by a skeptic; a **run** is one launch of the batch workflow; the **gather** composes a run's rungs; a **guard** is a test that passes before the change and after it. The **atomic runs** are the gate's compiled programs that run three times each at four threads.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it, and its quick checks under walk stay 7 of 7 for both programs.

**One consequential fork, for him before the launch: G, the grain size.** P-175's grain in the one library's parallel range can be tested only under walk today, and its value can be measured only on compiled reductions after the switch-over. (a) Build it now in rung P as a named constant, 16 for now, each chunk run by the sequential range's own methods. My trial kept both microGPT quick checks at 7 of 7, but the losses' last bits move by up to 4.4e-16 (tolerance 1e-12), and would move again if the measured value differs. (b) Leave it to the first batch after the switch-over, where PLAN had it: nothing changes under walk, and compiled loops split to single elements until then. I recommend (a); the record is written for it, and (b) strikes one step of P.
**D1 and D2:** no repair in scope needs either.
**Record:** `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-30.md`, one record in two runs, no `landsOnlyWith` anywhere. Twenty other forks land at their defaults (section 3).
**Run 1, climb batch 30:**
- **N:** the prelude's `RR64` and `RR32` take an integer numeral (row 442's numeral half); row 971, by initializing the component class on a pool thread in `MainWrapper` (my reproduction shows that a pool started earlier is not enough); walk's dead field-numeral code; row 960's reproducer rewritten; rows 958 and 967, and 974 if it fits.
- **P:** every forked arm joined (row 947); a task arm's locals and trailing block (rows 497 and 322's arm case, which forked arguments would otherwise turn into verify errors); a call's arguments forked (row 951); the grain size.
- **X:** the compiled transaction and the block's handler: rows 933, 934, 937, 888, 324, 949 (N3), 950 (N4), and N7 (row 466's note). This is row 933's home.
**Run 2, climb batch 30b, after run 1 lands:**
- **Y:** `tryatomic` compiled and under walk (rows 353, 952), the atomic expression (875), a mutable field in the transaction (319), row 322's remainder.
- **C:** rows 960 (parser), 963 (checker) and 957's second case (code generator).
**Why two runs:** X and Y would both edit `CodeGen.forAtomicBlock` and `Transaction.java`, and Y builds on X's handler. P and X share `CodeGen.java` and `BaseTask.java` by declaration; the record says where each puts new members.
**Tests today:** all compiled on the prelude with a program's own code, except the grain (walk) and N7 (a Java test of the store). Waiting for the switch-over: the one library's reductions compiled, the grain's measurement, array elements in transactions. Eight new programs join the atomic runs in run 1 (14 to 22) and three in run 2 (25); you add them to the script's list.
**Left out:** rows 973 and 966 (the ways review; a rung on them shares walk's `OverloadedFunction`, `Coercions` and `Numerals` with N and the `revival-numerals` Effect with N and C, so it runs after run 1); row 962 (contested) and row 446 (no rule on record); a contention policy; the review's "Can wait" list except row 952; row 442's non-numeral half.
**Disk:** 17.7 G free; the floor is 8.5 G for run 1 and 7 G for run 2. `/home/user/fortress-base31` is built at `9a0f69e01a` with `.base-ready` written, and `fortress-base30` is removed. Run 2 needs its own base build.
**Estimate:** run 1 about 5.5M tokens (4.4M to 7.0M), about 7 h; minutes N 160, P 210, X 210. Run 2 about 3.8M (3.1M to 5.0M), about 5 h 30 min; minutes Y 200, C 160.
**Edits wanted after the landings:** PLAN item 74 answered by X, items 78 and 79 by N, item 76 narrowed to rows 962 and 446, the phase 6 line on parallel reductions rewritten, phase 4's line on row 971 struck. Review-queue items 408, 488 and 489 answered, 449 reworded. Ledger closes and rewrites are listed per run in section 6, with the FACTS, POSITIONS and skill sentences made false.
**Not probed:** whether the analyzer forks the prelude's `gen` halves (P reports it) and row 322's remainder (Y reproduces it first). Y's and C's line numbers need a re-read on run 1's landed tree.
**Commits, pushed to the three refs:** `0a6abca6f0` (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-30/PROBES.md`) and `0829796281` (the record and its two INDEX lines).
